what_its_for: Dexamethasone is a steroid medicine that reduces swelling and calms down your immune system. Doctors use it to treat many conditions including severe allergies, asthma, arthritis, skin problems, certain types of cancer, brain swelling, and inflammation throughout the body. It can also help with nausea from chemotherapy and is sometimes used to treat COVID-19 in hospitalized patients.
how_to_take: Take dexamethasone exactly as your doctor tells you. It comes as a tablet, liquid, or eye drops depending on your prescription. Take the tablet or liquid by mouth with food or milk to protect your stomach. If you are taking the liquid form, measure your dose carefully using a special measuring spoon or syringe — never use a regular kitchen spoon. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, especially if you have been taking it for more than a few days, as this can cause serious side effects.
dosing: Your dose depends on your condition, age, weight, and how well you respond to treatment. Doses can range from as low as 0.5 mg to 20 mg or more per day. Your doctor may start you on a higher dose and slowly lower it over time. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and the label on your prescription bottle. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store dexamethasone tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections such as chickenpox, measles, or the flu, because dexamethasone can weaken your immune system and make it harder to fight infections. Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase the risk of stomach bleeding and ulcers. Do not get live vaccines (such as the shingles or nasal flu vaccine) while on this medication without your doctor's approval. Avoid eating large amounts of salty foods, as this medicine can cause your body to hold onto extra salt and water.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: signs of infection such as fever, chills, sore throat, or cough; unusual weight gain or swelling in your legs or ankles; high blood sugar symptoms such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision; mood or behavior changes such as depression, anxiety, or agitation; stomach pain or black/tarry stools; muscle weakness; vision problems or eye pain; or if you feel unusually tired or unwell. Also call your doctor before stopping this medication, as you may need to slowly taper your dose.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few hours to a few days of starting dexamethasone, depending on the condition being treated. For inflammation and allergic reactions, many people notice improvement within 1 to 2 days. For more serious conditions, it may take longer. Take this medicine for the full length of time prescribed, even if you feel better sooner.
special_populations: Elderly patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as bone loss, high blood sugar, and high blood pressure, so regular monitoring is important. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should only use dexamethasone if clearly needed and under close medical supervision. Children may experience slower growth with long-term use, so their doctor will monitor their height and weight regularly. Patients with diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease, liver disease, osteoporosis, or a history of stomach ulcers should inform their doctor before taking this medicine, as extra monitoring or dose adjustments may be needed.
